title: Roth IRA vs 401(k): Which Should You Use First?
custom_excerpt: Both are great retirement accounts, but the order you fund them in can be worth thousands, and one simple rule settles it.
meta_title: Roth IRA vs 401(k): Which Should You Use First? | Thrifty Crew
meta_description: Roth IRA or 401(k) first? Grab the full employer match, then fund the Roth for tax-free growth. A simple funding order, worked on a $60,000 salary.
lexical: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Here is a question I get more than almost any other. Someone finally has a little money left over at the end of the month, they want to start investing for retirement, and they hit a fork in the road. Roth IRA or 401(k)? Both are good. That is the good news. But if you can only fund one to start, the order matters more than most people think. Let me walk you through it in plain English, with real numbers.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The 401(k)","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"extended-heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"A 401(k) is the retirement plan your employer offers through payroll. Money comes out of your paycheck before you ever see it, which is half the reason it works. You cannot spend what never hits your checking account.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The traditional version is pre-tax. If you make $60,000 and put in $6,000, you are taxed as if you made $54,000 this year. That is a real, immediate discount on your tax bill. The money grows untouched for decades, and you pay ordinary income tax when you pull it out in retirement.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Here is the part that makes the 401(k) special, and it is the whole reason it goes first in this article. The match. Many employers will match your contributions up to a limit, often something like 50 cents on the dollar up to 6 percent of your pay, or dollar for dollar up to 3 or 4 percent. On that $60,000 salary, a dollar-for-dollar match up to 4 percent is $2,400 a year in free money. Nowhere else in personal finance do you get an instant 100 percent return. Not the stock market, not real estate, nowhere.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"In 2026 you can put up to $24,500 a year into a 401(k) if you are under 50. That is a high ceiling, more than most people will use.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The Roth IRA","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"extended-heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"A Roth IRA is an account you open yourself, at a brokerage, completely separate from your job. The word Roth means one thing above all else: you pay the tax now, and you never pay it again.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"You fund it with money you have already been taxed on. It grows for decades, and when you take it out in retirement, every dollar of growth comes out tax free. Put in $7,500 a year for 30 years and let it compound at a reasonable long-run average, and you could be looking at several hundred thousand dollars that the IRS cannot touch. That is a powerful thing to own when you are 65.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"In 2026 the Roth IRA limit is $7,500 if you are under 50. There is also an income cap. Single filers start losing the ability to contribute directly once income climbs past roughly $150,000, and it phases out completely a bit higher. Most working folks are nowhere near that, so it is a non-issue for the majority of people reading this.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"One quiet benefit people forget: because you already paid the tax, you can withdraw your contributions (the money you put in, not the growth) at any time without penalty. It is not a checking account and I would not treat it like one, but that flexibility is real.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The real difference","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"extended-heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Strip away the jargon and the whole thing comes down to a single question: do you pay the tax now, or do you pay it later?","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The traditional 401(k) says pay later. You get the deduction today, and you settle up with the IRS in retirement. The Roth IRA says pay now, and enjoy tax-free income for the rest of your life.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"So the honest answer depends on your tax rate today versus your tax rate in retirement. If you expect to be in a higher bracket later, the Roth wins because you locked in today's lower rate. If you are in your peak earning years and expect a lower bracket in retirement, the traditional 401(k) deduction is worth more.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The second difference is the match, and it breaks the tie every time at the start. The 401(k) has one. The Roth IRA does not. A 100 percent instant return beats any tax argument on the planet.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Which one is right for you","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"extended-heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Here is the order I give people, and it works for almost everyone.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":1,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"First, fund the 401(k) up to the full match.","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":" If your employer matches up to 4 percent, put in at least 4 percent. Not doing this is leaving a raise on the table. On a $60,000 salary that is $2,400 a year you are simply choosing not to take.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":1,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Second, once the match is captured, pivot to the Roth IRA.","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":" Fund it up to the $7,500 limit if you can. This is where you get your tax-free bucket going, and for younger workers especially, decades of tax-free growth is enormous.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":1,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Third, if you still have money left after maxing the Roth, go back and pump more into the 401(k)","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":" up to its higher limit.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The exception: if your employer offers no match at all, and you are early in your career in a low tax bracket, you can reasonably start with the Roth IRA first. Without a match, the 401(k) loses its trump card, and the tax-free growth of the Roth is a fine place to begin.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":1,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Bottom line:","type":"extended-text","version":1},{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":" Get the full 401(k) match first because free money wins, then fund a Roth IRA for tax-free growth, then come back and add more to the 401(k) if you can. Match, Roth, more 401(k). Follow that order and you are ahead of most people twice your income.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":2,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"This is general education, not personal advice, so check with a licensed professional about your situation.","type":"extended-text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":2,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Want the full playbook, plus every calculator, budget tool, and meal-prep recipe?
